definition: Extremal Ensemble Learning (EEL) is a machine learning algorithmic paradigm for graph partitioning.
details: EEL creates an ensemble of partitions and then uses information contained in the ensemble to find new and improved partitions. The ensemble evolves and learns how to form improved partitions through extremal updating procedure. The final solution is found by achieving consensus among its member partitions about what the optimal partition is.

explainer.lead: Extremal Ensemble Learning tackles graph partitioning by improving a collection of candidate partitions instead of relying on just one. It repeatedly updates that collection and finishes by forming a single answer through consensus among its members.

tiers.eli5: Imagine splitting a group of friends into teams and asking several people for their suggested teams. Instead of simply picking one suggestion, you use what the suggestions have in common to improve them. You keep doing this until the suggestions agree well enough to choose the final teams.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer applies EEL to graph partitioning by constructing multiple candidate partitions and using information across that ensemble to drive extremal updates. The evolving ensemble is central to the method, and the final output is a consensus partition rather than an arbitrary member.
tiers.paperLevel: For a graph G, let P = {p1, ..., pm} be an ensemble of partitions. EEL iteratively replaces P with an updated ensemble using an extremal updating procedure informed by its members, then derives the returned partition from consensus among those members.

explainer.example: Suppose nodes A through F must be divided into two groups, and two initial candidates are {A,B,C}|{D,E,F} and {A,B,D}|{C,E,F}. EEL uses information across such candidates during extremal updating; if the improved members converge on {A,B,C}|{D,E,F}, that consensus becomes the final partition.
explainer.intuition: Different candidate partitions can contain useful clues about a better division of a graph. EEL treats those candidates as an evolving ensemble, using their collective information to improve them before seeking agreement on a final partition.
howItWorks: Create an ensemble of candidate partitions of the graph.
Extract useful information from the ensemble.
Apply the extremal updating procedure to form improved partitions.
Produce the final partition through consensus among the members.
explainer.whyItMatters: EEL provides a way to refine graph partitions using an evolving population of solutions rather than depending on a single initial partition. Its consensus step then turns the improved ensemble into one final answer.
misconceptions: It is not just voting among a fixed set of partitions; the ensemble evolves through extremal updates.
It is a graph-partitioning paradigm, not a general method for combining predictive models.
Consensus among members is not, by itself, a guarantee of global optimality.
